# State of the Coast - Terschelling

## Introduction

The area of interest covers a section of Terschelling in the Netherlands, including its sandy, dune-dominated coastline and adjacent tidal waters. The assessed shoreline extends from the island’s southwestern coast across its central and northern sections toward the eastern end. Shoreline-change observations show substantial spatial variation, with both erosion and accretion occurring along this coast, as shown in Figure 1.

![Figure 1](data:image/png;base64,)

_Figure 1: Area of interest on Terschelling, showing shoreline-change rates and the locations of three transects._

## Historical Coastal Change

Historical shoreline change is mixed across the area of interest. Erosion categories account for 50.2% of the assessed shoreline: extreme erosion represents 25.0%, severe erosion 6.5%, intense erosion 14.3%, and erosion 4.4%. Stable conditions account for 23.4%.

Accretion categories account for 26.4% of the shoreline, including 12.4% classified as extreme accretion. Figure 1 shows that erosion and accretion are distributed in alternating sections along the coast rather than occurring uniformly. Figure 2 summarises the proportional distribution of the shoreline-change classifications.

![Figure 2](data:image/png;base64,)

_Figure 2: Distribution of shoreline-change-rate classes within the Terschelling area of interest._

## Transects

The three transects illustrate contrasting local shoreline trends (Figure 3). Transect 1 is located on the southwestern part of the assessed coast and shows a declining trend in distance along the transect. Its recorded shoreline-change rate is −5.94 m/year, classified as extreme erosion. The observations include several lower-distance values in the later part of the record, as well as two identified outliers.

Transects 2 and 3 are located along the central-to-northern section of the island. Both show increasing trends in distance along the transects. Transect 2 has a shoreline-change rate of 7.56 m/year, while Transect 3 has a rate of 7.49 m/year; both are classified as extreme accretion. The fitted trends for these two transects are supported by high coefficients of determination of 0.93 and 0.92, respectively.

![Figure 3](data:image/png;base64,)

_Figure 3: Historical shoreline-position observations, identified outliers, and fitted trends for the three Terschelling transects._

## Reports

The retrieved reference context provides methodological rather than Terschelling-specific information. A Deltares workflow description states that an area of interest is used to retrieve shoreline and transect information and notes that output quality depends on the quality of the underlying source data (Deltares, 2026). A separate Deltares shoreline-analysis memo describes the use of satellite imagery and automated processing to derive satellite-derived shorelines for historical shoreline assessment (Deltares, 2021). These references provide context for interpreting the mapped and transect-based shoreline observations but do not provide additional site-specific findings for Terschelling.

## Conclusion

The assessed Terschelling coastline is highly variable. Erosion is more prevalent than accretion overall, with extreme erosion forming the largest individual change-rate class. However, substantial accretion is also present, including extensive extreme accretion. The southwestern transect records a strong erosional trend, whereas the two central-to-northern transects record strong accretional trends. Together, these observations indicate pronounced differences in shoreline behaviour across the area of interest.
